beats.narration: The host opens an empty door.
Prize behind your door? Stay wins. Behind either other door? Switch wins.
We simulated a hundred and twenty games.
Switching wins two out of three times.

sources.claim: Switching wins two thirds of games when the host knows the prize location, always opens a different losing door and always offers the switch.
sources.ref: Steve Selvin, On the Monty Hall Problem (1975), The American Statistician. https://www.montyhallproblem.com/as.html

post.caption:
You pick one of three doors. The host knows where the prize is, always opens a different door that’s empty, and always offers you the switch. Would you take it?

Switching wins whenever your first pick misses. With the prize equally likely behind each door, the exact chances are 1 in 3 for staying and 2 in 3 for switching.

In our 120-game simulation, staying won 34 games (28.3%) and switching won 86 (71.7%).
